video_title: Lawfare Daily: The U.S. Withdrawal from Iraq, and the Future of the Iraq-U.S. Relationship
gist: Panel (Victoria Taylor, an ambassador, Omar Muhammad) on the US troop exit from Iraq: Trump's transactional posture, dollar-transfer pressure, militias that will not disarm and Iran's Hormuz chokehold on Iraqi oil leave Iraq a battleground whose path depends on US-Iran escalation. They dispute whether engagement or system rehabilitation is viable.

themes.theme: US withdrawal terms and the unresolved post-troop security relationship

insights.claim: The Biden-negotiated 2024 timeline ended Operation Inherent Resolve in federal Iraq by Sept 2025 and in the Kurdistan region by Sept 2026; the Trump administration has now fully departed, and what a future bilateral security presence looks like is unanswered. The US consulate in Erbil remains largely empty after evacuating during Iran-war drone and rocket attacks.
insights.speaker: Victoria Taylor
insights.so_what: Sets the baseline: no US military presence beyond diplomats, and Kurdistan exposure is now unprotected.

insights.claim: Biden saw the end of Inherent Resolve as the start of a continuing bilateral security relationship; the Trump administration treats security ties as non-continuous, existing only where a narrow risk-versus-reward test favors the US.
insights.speaker: Victoria Taylor
insights.so_what: Expect transactional, reversible US commitments in Iraq and likely across the region.

insights.claim: The Trump administration is using pauses in security assistance and in dollar transfers (paused this spring) as levers to push Baghdad to act against militias; the approach to Iraqi commercial ties is stick-heavy.
insights.speaker: Victoria Taylor
insights.so_what: The dollar channel is the main US coercive tool over Iraq; watch Fed/Treasury access for Iraqi banks and oil revenue.
insights.quote: The dollar and US economic tools remain a lever that the Trump administration is prepared to use

insights.claim: The withdrawal fits a Trump vision of a Middle East where the US is not the major security guarantor and regional states carry more security responsibility, even as the US is in a prolonged military conflict with Iran alongside Israel.
insights.speaker: Victoria Taylor
insights.so_what: US retrenchment paired with active war with Iran implies more regional burden-sharing and more volatility for Gulf states.

insights.claim: The Iran war disrupted the NATO mission in Iraq, which largely departed amid militia and Iranian attacks; whether the Turkish military and NATO presence become targets of Iraqi sovereignty politics is an open question.
insights.speaker: Victoria Taylor
insights.so_what: Western security presence in Iraq could shrink further beyond US troops.

insights.claim: Withdrawal policy in Iraq has been bipartisan: the 2011 exit was agreed by George W. Bush in Dec 2008, the 2026 timeline by Biden. American appetite for troops there declines the longer they stay, so it is not a contested political issue absent a new security incident.
insights.speaker: Ambassador Doug (Arab Gulf States Institute)
insights.so_what: Do not price a US troop return as a base case; it takes a major shock.

themes.theme: Iraqi capability gaps and militia risk after withdrawal

insights.claim: After 2011 the US shifted to a larger embassy military assistance office and focused training on the Counterterrorism Service, the force with the greatest US advantage; CTS bore the brunt of fighting ISIS in 2014 when the army collapsed.
insights.speaker: Ambassador Doug (Arab Gulf States Institute)
insights.so_what: Shows concentrated, small-footprint training can work, but depends on the capable unit surviving politically.

insights.claim: Iraq's most acute weakness is air defense; Iran-backed militias have hit oil fields in the Kurdistan region and around Basra and attacked targets in Saudi Arabia, UAE, Kuwait and Jordan, and Iraq cannot militarily counter this, leaving only political discouragement of militias.
insights.speaker: Ambassador Doug (Arab Gulf States Institute)
insights.so_what: Energy infrastructure in Iraq and the Gulf stays exposed to cheap drone attacks; a risk premium on regional oil assets persists.

insights.claim: Militias take direction, training and supply from the IRGC, with apparent cooperation through Tehran with the Houthis, to pressure international oil markets.
insights.speaker: Ambassador Doug (Arab Gulf States Institute)
insights.so_what: Militia attacks are an oil-price lever coordinated across the axis, not just local violence.

insights.claim: Militias will not disarm because their orders come from Tehran, not Baghdad; they will frame the US exit as a resistance victory, and Iraqi PM al-Zaidi's disarmament pledge (deadline reportedly June 30 next year, already shifted once) is unlikely to be met.
insights.speaker: Omar Muhammad
insights.so_what: Fade headlines on militia disarmament; the deadline is a catalyst for slippage rather than resolution.
insights.quote: the militias will never leave their arms

insights.claim: The new PM reportedly came to power through a bargain involving PMF chair Faleh al-Fayyad, though the relationship is more complicated than being in their pocket.
insights.speaker: Omar Muhammad
insights.so_what: Limits the PM's room to confront the PMF.

insights.claim: The militias' new risk is dragging Iraq into being a launch base against neighbors (drones at UAE and Saudi Arabia); Gulf states will not wait for Baghdad to order its house, and any renewed escalation could quickly become a disaster inside Iraq.
insights.speaker: Omar Muhammad
insights.so_what: Raises odds of Gulf retaliation or spillover into Iraq, with oil-supply implications.

insights.claim: The Kurdistan region may become a bigger target after US departure because Iran has long seen Kurdistan as a Mossad agent rather than just a US partner.
insights.speaker: Omar Muhammad
insights.so_what: Erbil-based energy and commercial interests face more risk without the US presence.

insights.claim: In Ninevah province, militias now hold essentially 100 percent economic control, replacing the ISIS economy, especially after regime change in Syria, across Christian and Muslim areas alike.
insights.speaker: Omar Muhammad
insights.so_what: Militias' economic capture is the mechanism that makes disarmament unrealistic and complicates any investment in the north.

insights.claim: Iraq's CTS has lost the independence it had in the Mosul battle: its commander was sacked and it is accused of being a US puppet, undermining the one capable force.
insights.speaker: Omar Muhammad
insights.so_what: Erodes the best counter-ISIS option, a risk for ISIS resurgence.

themes.theme: Iraq as Iranian lever and the oil and economic exposure

insights.claim: Iraq is both tool and victim of Iran in the war: the IRGC uses Iraqi militias against enemies, particularly in Kurdistan, and Iran has stopped most Iraqi oil from transiting the Strait of Hormuz.
insights.speaker: Ambassador Doug (Arab Gulf States Institute)
insights.so_what: Iraqi crude is effectively removed from the market, supporting global prices while Iraq's finances deteriorate.

insights.claim: Iraq is the Gulf state most hurt by Hormuz closure because it lacks the trillion-dollar sovereign wealth buffers that Kuwait or Qatar have to survive years until bypass routes are built.
insights.speaker: Ambassador Doug (Arab Gulf States Institute)
insights.so_what: Iraq fiscal stress and arrears risk are acute; Kuwait and Qatar can ride out disruption.
insights.quote: Iraq does not have the buffer of a trillion dollar sovereign wealth fund

insights.claim: Iraq depends on oil for over 90 percent of government revenue, so diversification is key to jobs and a sustainable economy.
insights.speaker: Victoria Taylor
insights.so_what: Iraqi budget is a near-pure oil-price and export-volume play.

insights.claim: US companies will only invest if deals are profitable; the US government controls the sticks, not the carrots. Militia attacks on oil fields and Hormuz closure undermine Iraq as an investment destination even if oil can be extracted.
insights.speaker: Victoria Taylor
insights.so_what: Do not expect US corporate investment in Iraq to follow rhetoric (PM al-Zaidi: US troops leave but US companies stay) until security and export routes improve.
insights.quote: the US government doesn't control the carrots. The private sector controls the carrots.

insights.claim: The Trump national security strategy argued the Middle East matters less because the US produces its own oil, but the Iran war shows global oil prices still hit American consumers.
insights.speaker: Victoria Taylor
insights.so_what: Undermines the premise of US energy independence insulating the US from Gulf disruption.

themes.theme: Iraq's political system and the limits of the US approach

insights.claim: Since 2003 US administrations of both parties have anchored on keeping the Iraqi government running regardless of ISIS territorial control, destroyed cities or militia economic domination, which has repeatedly produced the opposite result and empowered militias tied to Iran.
insights.speaker: Omar Muhammad
insights.so_what: Each new reformist prime minister (Abadi, Kadhimi, now a young banker) is a repeat bet; fade reform narratives.

insights.claim: Reformist prime ministers have failed in sequence: Abadi institutionalized the PMF, Kadhimi resigned after drones were sent to his house, and now a young banker PM is marketed as a reformer; the system itself, not individuals, is the problem and a sectarian order has taken root.
insights.speaker: Omar Muhammad
insights.so_what: Personality-driven reform stories in Iraq have poor track records.
insights.quote: The issue is not these individuals. The issue is that the entire system itself is rigged.

insights.claim: After the November election, a group of 12 Shia political leaders chose the prime minister among themselves with almost no connection to the vote count; state institutions are disconnected from the public.
insights.speaker: Victoria Taylor
insights.so_what: Election results are a poor guide to who rules Iraq; political risk comes from elite bargains.

insights.claim: Iraqis broadly expected the US to refrain from backing the regime during the 2018-19 protests, not to police streets; US diplomats then ended up photographed with militia figures such as Qais al-Khazali.
insights.speaker: Omar Muhammad
insights.so_what: Credibility of US engagement among Iraqis is low, limiting soft power in a militia-dominated state.

insights.claim: The Ambassador argues the US cannot provide ground security; it works through institutions, and in 2018-19 it was not realistic to have US forces fight the PMF shooting protesters.
insights.speaker: Ambassador Doug (Arab Gulf States Institute)
insights.so_what: US policy stays institution-based and non-kinetic towards militias absent attacks on US targets.

insights.claim: Many Kurds, Christians, Yazidis and educated urban Sunnis and Shia saw US troops as security for their communities, and many Iraqis did not want Trump to remove troops, although the Ambassador doubts US troops ever constrained Iran or the militias.
insights.speaker: Ambassador Doug (Arab Gulf States Institute)
insights.so_what: Minority communities and Kurdistan are the most exposed to the security vacuum.

insights.claim: Iraq's trajectory over the next year depends on the US-Iran conflict, not Iraqi politics; a prolonged conflict will have dramatic negative effects on Iraq's security and economy.
insights.speaker: Victoria Taylor
insights.so_what: Treat Iraq risk as a derivative of US-Iran escalation.
insights.quote: Iraq is not in full control of its own destiny right now.

insights.claim: The Ambassador hopes for Iraqi economic integration: a better banking system, and Iraqis who hold money abroad investing at home; he will not focus on security unless violence returns as in 2018-19.
insights.speaker: Ambassador Doug (Arab Gulf States Institute)
insights.so_what: Banking reform and capital repatriation are the constructive signals.

insights.claim: Omar opposes banking support for Iraq now, arguing it would enrich militias, and expects an eventual US-Iran escalation to spiral out of control, with Iraqi militias refusing to stay restrained when Iran calls on them.
insights.speaker: Omar Muhammad
insights.so_what: Contrarian to the engagement case; implies sanctions and dollar access around Iraqi banks remain contested and escalation risk is underpriced.

insights.claim: The US should pursue a normal diplomatic relationship with Iraq not tied to troops, including normal security cooperation and educational and commercial exchanges, because the transformative 2003 vision failed but what happens in Iraq does not stay in Iraq.
insights.speaker: Victoria Taylor
insights.so_what: The advocated middle path is the opposite of the current transactional approach; policy debate to watch.
